definition:
A covenant is a binding relationship established by a solemn commitment. It joins two parties with promises and obligations, it is sealed by an oath and often by a sign or a sacrifice, and it carries consequences for faithfulness and for betrayal. Ancient people made covenants between kings and peoples, between neighbors, and between husband and wife. The astonishing claim of the Bible is that God binds himself this way to human beings. He makes covenants with Noah and every living creature, with Abraham, with Israel at Sinai, with David, and finally the new covenant promised by Jeremiah and sealed, Jesus says, in his own blood. Following these covenants is one of the surest ways to follow the whole Bible as one story, because each one advances God's purpose to have a people who are his and to be their God. The refrain of that purpose sounds from Leviticus, “I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people” (Leviticus 26:12), to the Bible's last pages, “They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3).

The Hebrew word is berit, which occurs about 287 times in the Old Testament. Its origin is uncertain and debated, and its meaning comes from how it is used, not from any proposed root. Hebrew speaks of ‘cutting’ a covenant (karat berit), an idiom tied to rites in which animals were cut in two (Genesis 15:10, 18; Jeremiah 34:18). Covenants bind people to each other: Abraham and Abimelech (Genesis 21:27), Jacob and Laban (Genesis 31:44), Jonathan and David (1 Samuel 18:3), and a husband and wife (Malachi 2:14; Proverbs 2:17). Closely related words include ’alah, ‘oath’ or ‘sworn curse’, and chesed, the steadfast loyalty that keeps covenant, which the Berean Standard Bible renders ‘loving devotion’ (Deuteronomy 7:9). The Greek translation of the Old Testament, the Septuagint, almost always renders berit with diathēkē, a word that in ordinary Greek meant a will or testament, rather than synthēkē, an agreement between equals. Many scholars think the choice suited covenants that God initiates and grants. Diathēkē occurs 33 times in the New Testament, 17 of them in Hebrews, and through the Latin testamentum it gave the church the names Old Testament and New Testament.
ot:
The word berit first appears when God tells Noah before the flood, “I will establish My covenant with you” (Genesis 6:18). The first three chapters of Genesis do not use it, and whether God's relationship with Adam was a covenant is debated. Hosea 6:7 says, “But they, like Adam, have transgressed the covenant”, and interpreters read ‘Adam’ there as the first man, as humankind generally, or as the town of Adam by the Jordan (Joshua 3:16). After the flood God makes his covenant with Noah, his descendants, and “every living creature” (Genesis 9:10), promising never again to destroy the earth by flood and setting the rainbow as “the sign of the covenant” (Genesis 9:12). It is universal in scope, it depends on God's promise alone, and it frames all later history: God will preserve the world in which he will work out his rescue.

The covenant with Abraham is the root of everything after. God promises land, offspring, and blessing: “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). In Genesis 15, after Abram believes God and it is “credited to him as righteousness” (15:6), God seals the promise in an ancient form. Animals are cut in two, and in the dark “a smoking firepot and a flaming torch appeared and passed between the halves” (15:17). In such rites the parties who walked between the pieces called the fate of the animals on themselves if they broke their word (compare Jeremiah 34:18). Here God alone passes through, binding himself while Abram sleeps. In Genesis 17 God calls Abraham to “Walk before Me and be blameless” (17:1), promises “to be your God and the God of your descendants after you” (17:7), and gives circumcision as “a sign of the covenant” (17:11), for the household and for every male child at eight days old (17:12). Promise and obligation belong together, and the promise comes first. When Israel groans in Egypt, the exodus begins because God “remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (Exodus 2:24).

At Sinai God first reminds Israel of rescue, “I carried you on eagles' wings and brought you to Myself”, and then offers covenant: “if you will indeed obey My voice and keep My covenant, you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations”, and “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:4-6). The Ten Commandments begin with grace, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 20:2). Moses reads the Book of the Covenant, the people pledge obedience, and he sprinkles them with blood, saying, “This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you” (Exodus 24:8); then the elders eat and drink in God's presence (24:11). The Sabbath is its sign (Exodus 31:16-17). Israel breaks the covenant almost at once with the golden calf, and God renews it by mercy (Exodus 34:10, 27-28). Deuteronomy restates the covenant on the plains of Moab for a new generation (Deuteronomy 29:1), sets out blessings and curses (Deuteronomy 28), and looks past Israel's failure to a day when “The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts” (Deuteronomy 30:6). Since George Mendenhall's studies in 1954, scholars have compared Sinai and Deuteronomy with Hittite treaties of the later second millennium BC, which move from a preamble and historical prologue to stipulations, witnesses, and blessings and curses; others compare Deuteronomy with Neo-Assyrian treaties such as Esarhaddon's of 672 BC. Scholars disagree about which parallels fit best and what they imply for dating, but the comparison shows that Israel understood its relation to God in the familiar form of a great king's covenant with his people. The covenant was renewed under Joshua at Shechem (Joshua 24:25), under King Josiah about 622 BC (2 Kings 23:3), and after the exile (Nehemiah 9:38). God also made a lasting covenant of priesthood with Phinehas and Levi (Numbers 25:12-13; Malachi 2:4-5).

To David God promises a dynasty: “I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his Father, and he will be My son” (2 Samuel 7:13-14). A son who sins will be disciplined, but God's loving devotion will not be taken away (7:14-15). Second Samuel 7 does not use the word covenant, but David calls it “an everlasting covenant” (2 Samuel 23:5), and the psalms do too (Psalm 89:3-4; 132:11-12). Psalm 89 then laments the throne cast down, and the exile seemed to end the promise. The prophets charge Israel and Judah with breaking the covenant (Jeremiah 11:10) and bring God's case against them like a lawsuit (Micah 6:2), and the exile falls as the covenant curses warned (Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28). Yet God promises that even in exile he will “remember My covenant with Jacob” (Leviticus 26:42). Jeremiah announces “a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah”, unlike the one broken at Sinai: “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts”, and “they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest”, for “I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more” (Jeremiah 31:31-34). Ezekiel promises an everlasting “covenant of peace” with God's sanctuary among his people (Ezekiel 37:26; compare 36:26-27), Isaiah offers to all who come “an everlasting covenant— My loving devotion promised to David” (Isaiah 55:3) and speaks of a servant appointed “to be a covenant for the people and a light to the nations” (Isaiah 42:6), and Malachi, at the end of the prophets, foresees the coming of “the Messenger of the covenant” (Malachi 3:1).
nt:
The New Testament opens with Zechariah praising God, who has come “to remember His holy covenant, the oath He swore to our father Abraham” (Luke 1:72-73). On the night before he died, Jesus took the cup at the Passover meal and said, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you” (Luke 22:20; compare 1 Corinthians 11:25). In Matthew the words are “This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28). The phrase echoes Moses at Sinai, “the blood of the covenant” (Exodus 24:8), and the promise of forgiveness echoes Jeremiah's new covenant (Jeremiah 31:34). Jesus rarely used the word covenant, but at the decisive hour he interpreted his death as the sacrifice that establishes the covenant the prophets promised, and the church has repeated his words at the Lord's Table ever since. Peter tells the crowd in the temple that they are “sons of the prophets and of the covenant” God made with Abraham, and that God sent his Servant “first to you to bless you” (Acts 3:25-26).

Paul calls himself and his coworkers “ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6). In 2 Corinthians 3 he contrasts the fading glory on Moses' face with the lasting glory of the Spirit's ministry, in which believers are being changed into the Lord's image. In Galatians 3 he argues that the covenant with Abraham, ratified by God, could not be annulled by “The law that came 430 years later” (Galatians 3:17). The promise was spoken to Abraham's seed, and Paul reads the singular as pointing to Christ (3:16), so that “if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise” (3:29), and through him the blessing of Abraham reaches the Gentiles along with the promised Spirit (3:14). In Galatians 4:24 he uses Hagar and Sarah as a figure of two covenants, Sinai bearing children for slavery and the promise bearing children for freedom. To Gentile believers he writes that they were once “strangers to the covenants of the promise, without hope and without God in the world” (Ephesians 2:12), and now are brought near by the blood of Christ. Yet he insists that to Israel belong “the covenants” (Romans 9:4), and in Romans 11 he writes that “all Israel will be saved”, quoting Isaiah on the Deliverer from Zion and adding, “this is My covenant with them when I take away their sins” (Romans 11:26-27). “God's gifts and His call are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). How these chapters bear on the future of the Jewish people is one of the questions the covenant frameworks answer differently.

Hebrews gives covenant its fullest New Testament treatment. Jesus is “the guarantee of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22), the mediator of a covenant “founded on better promises” (8:6). The writer quotes Jeremiah 31:31-34 in full (Hebrews 8:8-12), the longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament, and concludes, “By speaking of a new covenant, He has made the first one obsolete” (8:13). The Sinai covenant was inaugurated with blood (9:18-20), and Christ's own blood inaugurates the new, so that he is “the mediator of a new covenant” and those who are called may receive the eternal inheritance (9:15). In 9:16-17 the writer plays on the double sense of diathēkē as covenant and will; most English Bibles translate it ‘will’ there, while some scholars argue that ‘covenant’ is meant throughout, referring to the death of the sacrificial victim. The letter ends with a blessing from “the God of peace, who through the blood of the eternal covenant brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus” (13:20).

The Bible's last vision gathers the covenant promise into one sentence: “the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3). The promise first spoken to Abraham, repeated at Sinai, and renewed through Jeremiah and Ezekiel is fulfilled in the new creation, where the covenant God lives among his people forever. Along the way the New Testament adds no new covenant beyond the one Jesus sealed. It announces that the covenants have reached their goal in him: he is the seed of Abraham, the faithful Israelite, the son of David, and the mediator of the new covenant, and all God's promises find their “Yes” in him (2 Corinthians 1:20).

keyTexts.why: God's covenant with Noah and every living creature, sealed with the rainbow. A promise to preserve the world, resting on God's word alone.
Abram believes and is counted righteous, and God alone passes between the cut animals, binding himself by oath to give the land to Abram's descendants.
The covenant with Abraham confirmed: to be God to him and his descendants, the call to walk blamelessly, and circumcision as the covenant sign.
God reminds Israel that he rescued them and offers covenant: his treasured possession, a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation.
The Sinai covenant is ratified with the blood of the covenant, and the elders eat and drink before God. Jesus' words over the cup echo this scene.
Beyond the curses of exile, God promises to restore his people and circumcise their hearts so that they love him. A seed of the new covenant.
God promises David a house, a kingdom, and a throne forever, and to be a Father to his son. The root of the hope for a messianic king.
The covenant with David celebrated as unbreakable, followed in the rest of the psalm by lament that it seems to have failed. Faith holding God to his word.
The promise of a new covenant: the law written on the heart, every member knowing the LORD, and sins forgiven and remembered no more.
God promises to cleanse his people, give them a new heart, and put his Spirit within them, joining covenant renewal to the Spirit's work.
At the Passover Jesus gives the cup as the new covenant in his blood, interpreting his death as the sacrifice that establishes the covenant Jeremiah promised.
Paul contrasts the ministry of the old covenant with the Spirit-given ministry of the new, which changes believers into the Lord's image.
The promise to Abraham cannot be annulled by the later law. It is fulfilled in Christ, the seed, and all who belong to him are Abraham's heirs.
Jesus mediates a better covenant on better promises. Hebrews quotes Jeremiah 31 in full and calls the first covenant obsolete.
The covenant formula fulfilled in the new creation: God dwells with his people, they are his people, and he is their God.

history:
The early church read the covenants as one story that led to Christ, though it described that story in different ways. Irenaeus of Lyons (about 180) spoke of four principal covenants given to humanity, in the Latin text of his work those under Adam, Noah, Moses, and the gospel (Against Heresies 3.11.8), and he argued against Marcion and the gnostics that the God of the covenants with Israel is the Father of Jesus Christ. Marcion, who taught in Rome around 144, had rejected the Old Testament and its God, and the church's refusal of his teaching was a refusal to cut the new covenant loose from the old. Other early writers drew a harsher line. The Epistle of Barnabas, from the early second century, claimed that Israel lost the covenant at Sinai when Moses broke the tablets and that it belongs to Christians alone. That view, and the contempt for Jews that grew with it in some later Christian preaching, left a long and shameful legacy.

Covenant became a central organizing idea during the Reformation. Huldrych Zwingli in Zurich defended the baptism of infants against the Anabaptists in the 1520s by arguing for the unity of the covenant with Abraham and the covenant in Christ, and Heinrich Bullinger's treatise on the one and eternal covenant of God (1534) set out that unity at length. John Calvin devoted two chapters of the Institutes (2.10 and 2.11) to the likeness and the differences between the Old and New Testaments, teaching that the covenant with the patriarchs is in substance the same as ours and differs in its administration. Later Reformed theologians developed the framework further. Zacharias Ursinus spoke of a covenant of creation (1562), Dudley Fenner was the first to print the phrase ‘covenant of works’ (1585), and the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646, chapter 7) confessed a covenant of works made with Adam and a covenant of grace offered to sinners in Christ, administered differently under the law and the gospel. Johannes Cocceius (1648) and Herman Witsius (The Economy of the Covenants, 1677) wrote major works of what came to be called federal theology, from the Latin foedus, ‘covenant’. The Particular Baptists' Second London Confession (1677, reissued 1689) kept much of Westminster's language while teaching that the covenant of grace was revealed step by step in the Old Testament and formally established in the new covenant, which is why they baptized only believers. Lutheran theology, by contrast, organized its teaching more around the distinction between law and gospel than around a covenant scheme.

In the nineteenth century John Nelson Darby, a leader of the Plymouth Brethren from the 1830s, taught a different reading of the whole Bible as a series of dispensations in which God keeps distinct purposes for Israel and the church. The Scofield Reference Bible (1909) carried this dispensationalism into many American churches, Dallas Theological Seminary (founded 1924) became its academic center, and Charles Ryrie's Dispensationalism Today (1965) named the distinction between Israel and the church its essential mark. Progressive dispensationalists, notably Craig Blaising and Darrell Bock (Progressive Dispensationalism, 1993), later stressed more continuity. In the twentieth century biblical scholarship studied covenant against its ancient background: George Mendenhall's comparison with Hittite treaties (1954), Meredith Kline's Treaty of the Great King (1963) on Deuteronomy, and Moshe Weinfeld's distinction between obligatory treaties and promissory royal grants (1970), which he applied to the covenants with Abraham and David. E. P. Sanders's Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977) described the Judaism of Paul's day as ‘covenantal nomism’, a religion in which obedience to the law was the response to God's gracious covenant rather than the means of entering it, and reopened discussion of Paul and the law. The Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate (1965, section 4), citing Romans 11:28-29, taught that God does not take back the gifts he gave the Jews, a statement many Protestant churches have echoed. More recently, Peter Gentry and Stephen Wellum's Kingdom through Covenant (2012) set out progressive covenantalism, and Tom Wells and Fred Zaspel's New Covenant Theology (2002) set out the view of that name. The site's page on covenant frameworks compares these readings in detail.

differ.body: Covenant theology reads Scripture through a covenant of works with Adam, broken in the fall, and a single covenant of grace running from the promise of Genesis 3:15 through Abraham, Moses, and David to Christ. The covenant with Abraham, “to be your God and the God of your descendants” (Genesis 17:7), is the same covenant believers enjoy now; its administration has changed but its substance has not, and saints in every age are saved by grace through faith in the promised Christ. There is one people of God, one olive tree into which Gentiles are grafted (Romans 11:17-24), and the church is its continuation, not its replacement. Because the covenant sign was given to believers and their children, and Peter says the promise is “to you and your children” (Acts 2:39), baptism is given to the children of believers. The Westminster Confession, Geerhardus Vos, and Michael Horton represent this view.

Many Reformed Baptists, following the Second London Confession (1677/1689), share the classic framework of a covenant of works and a covenant of grace but hold that the covenant of grace was promised and revealed in the Old Testament covenants and formally established only in the new covenant. The covenants with Abraham and Moses had an earthly, national side, with land, a nation, and physical descent, that pointed forward to Christ. The new covenant, unlike the old, is made with people who all “know Me, from the least of them to the greatest” (Jeremiah 31:34), and its members are those born of the Spirit. The sign of the new covenant therefore goes to those who profess faith, and the continuity of the one people of God is found in Christ, not in households by birth.

Dispensationalists read the Bible as the unfolding of distinct administrations, or dispensations, in which God deals with humanity in different ways, and they hold that Israel and the church are distinct peoples in God's purpose. God's unconditional promises to Abraham and David, including the land from “the river of Egypt to the great River Euphrates” (Genesis 15:18) and an everlasting throne, will be fulfilled to the nation of Israel as the original hearers understood them, and Romans 11:26 promises a future turning of ethnic Israel. The church, born at Pentecost, shares in the spiritual blessings of the new covenant now. Classic dispensationalists (Darby, Scofield, Ryrie) drew the lines sharply; progressive dispensationalists (Blaising and Bock) stress one inaugurated kingdom and see the church already sharing new covenant blessings, while still expecting a future for national Israel.

Progressive covenantalists trace the covenants Scripture names, with Noah, Abraham, Israel, David, and the new covenant, and argue that each builds on the last and reaches its goal in Christ. They are cautious about the theological categories of a covenant of works and one covenant of grace, preferring to follow the biblical covenants as they progress, and they read Israel, the land, and the temple as types fulfilled in Christ and the new creation. With covenant theology they hold that there is one people of God in Christ, since “if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's seed” (Galatians 3:29); with Baptists they hold that the new covenant community is made up of believers, so baptism follows profession of faith. Peter Gentry and Stephen Wellum set out the view in Kingdom through Covenant (2012).

New covenant theology focuses on the relation of the Christian to the law of Moses. It holds that the Mosaic covenant was given as a single unit to Israel for a set time and was fulfilled and brought to its end in Christ, so that believers live under “the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2; 1 Corinthians 9:21), the will of God as taught by Jesus and his apostles. Much of the old law reappears there, deepened, but it binds Christians as Christ's command rather than as the Sinai covenant. Hebrews calls the first covenant “obsolete” (Hebrews 8:13), and Paul lists the Sabbath among the shadows whose substance is Christ (Colossians 2:16-17), so the weekly Sabbath is not binding as law. Tom Wells and Fred Zaspel's New Covenant Theology (2002) is a standard statement.

errors:
The church rejected Marcion's claim that the covenants with Israel came from a lesser god and that Christians should discard the Old Testament. The God who swore to Abraham is the Father of Jesus Christ, and the new covenant is the fulfillment of promises made to Israel, not their abolition. The church has also come, often too slowly, to reject the hard supersessionism voiced in writings like the Epistle of Barnabas, the claim that God has cast off the Jewish people and revoked his covenant with them, and the contempt for Jews that it helped feed across centuries. Paul's own words stand against it: “God's gifts and His call are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). Christians still differ on how Israel and the church relate, but none of the frameworks above teaches that God has abandoned the Jewish people. Most confessing churches have also declined the opposite proposal, sometimes called two-covenant theology, that Jews are saved through the Sinai covenant apart from Jesus, since the apostles preached him as Israel's Messiah “first to the Jew” (Romans 1:16).

Two distortions recur within the church. One treats covenant as a contract in which people earn God's favor by keeping their side. But every biblical covenant begins with God's initiative and grace: the rainbow after the flood, the torch between the pieces, the exodus before the commandments. The other treats covenant membership as a guarantee that needs no faith or obedience, as when Judah trusted in the chant ‘the temple of the LORD’ (Jeremiah 7:4) and John the Baptist warned the crowds not to say, “We have Abraham as our father” (Matthew 3:9). The covenants join promise and obligation; the obligation is the grateful answer of those whom God has already claimed.
life:
Covenant means that God has bound himself by his word. The Christian's security does not rest on the strength of his or her own grip but on the oath of the God who passed between the pieces and who sealed the new covenant with the blood of his Son. That is why believers can pray on the basis of promises, as Moses, David, and the psalmists did, reminding God of what he has said. It also means that faith is lived out in faithfulness. Covenant love, chesed, is loyalty that holds when feelings fade, and God calls his people to show it to him and to one another, most visibly in marriage, which Scripture calls a covenant, and in the life of the church.

The Lord's Supper places the covenant at the center of Christian worship. Each time the church hears “This cup is the new covenant in My blood”, it is reminded that its life together rests on a sacrifice already made and a promise already kept. And covenant gives believers a place in a very old story. The promise to Abraham, the law at Sinai, the throne of David, and the hope of the prophets are family history for everyone who belongs to Christ, and they point toward the day when God will dwell with his people and be their God.
questions: In Genesis 15 God alone passes between the pieces of the animals. What does that scene teach about how God relates to his people, and how does it shape the way you read the rest of the covenants?
Jeremiah says the new covenant will not be like the covenant made at Sinai (Jeremiah 31:32). What exactly is new about it, and what continues from the older covenants?

Christians who hold different covenant frameworks agree that the whole Bible leads to Christ. How does that shared conviction help believers read the Old Testament, and how might it help them disagree well?
